dynorphin, a peptide that is colocalized with the neurotransmitter acetylcholine in the brain, has the same effects on drinking as morphine and that these effects are not primarily mediated through activation at kappa opioid receptors.
the endogenous opioid peptide, dynorphin, is involved in the regulation of water balance and that this function is not mediated through activation of kappa opioid receptors.
the selective kappa opioid agonists, ethylketocylazocine and U50, 4,88H, are more potent inhibitors of drinking than are the non-selective agonists, morphine and [D-Pen 2, D-Pep 5]enkepahalin.

the role of endogenous opioids in the control of ingestive behavior and the mechanisms by which these substances mediate their behavioral effects.
the role of endogenous opioids in the homeostasis of water balance.
the role of opioid peptides in the regulation of water intake.

dynorphin-(l-13) and the mu agonist, morphine, are the most potent centrally-acting opioid agonists to inhibit drinking in the 14 hr deprived rat.
